title: throughput-benchmarking-harness-and-methodology
content:
Purpose:
This doc describes the recommended throughput benchmarking harness and methodology used for serving-runtime performance investigations (profiling, bottlenecks, and benchmarks). The goal is repeatable, comparable measurements of steady-state throughput and meaningful diagnostics for regressions.

Scope:
- Focus: throughput-oriented benchmarks for the inference serving runtime (tokens/sec, requests/sec at target SLOs)
- Not covered in detail: qualitative output quality, cost modeling beyond tokens-per-second, or client SDK microbenchmarks (except where they affect loadgen).

Goals / Success criteria:
- Repeatable runs (same inputs + environment -> similar metrics within a small tolerance)
- Actionable signals: identify whether bottleneck is GPU compute, memory bandwidth, batching logic, driver/kernel compilation, host networking, or client-side limits
- Baseline and regression tests that can be automated in CI for PRs that touch serving or runtime kernels

High level methodology:
1) Fix the software stack (runtime commit, model artifact checksum, container image). Document exact CUDA, cuDNN, Triton/TVM/XLA, and driver versions.
2) Use deterministic, seeded input sets and a documented request distribution (sequence lengths, batchable prompts, KV-reuse patterns).
3) Warm up to steady-state before collecting measurements.
4) Measure during a defined steady-state window and collect full telemetry (latency percentiles, tokens/sec, GPU metrics, host metrics, per-batch stats, trace samples).
5) Repeat runs (>= 3) and report mean+stdev.

Benchmark metrics to collect:
- Primary: tokens/sec (generated tokens/sec), requests/sec (for non-tokenized response workloads)
- Latency: p50/p90/p95/p99 for overall request and for first-byte/last-byte where applicable
- Resource: GPU utilization (SM %), GPU memory usage, GPU power, GPU PCIe throughput, CPU utilization, context-switches, network egress, open sockets
- Runtime internal: average batch size, queue length, KV cache hit/miss, kernel time vs overhead, compile time (if JIT), kernel launch latencies
- Errors: timeouts, 5xx responses, partial outputs

Load generator design decisions:
- Open-loop vs closed-loop: prefer open-loop (fixed RPS) for exploring max throughput; use closed-loop (concurrency-driven) for SLO-focused latency tests.
- Persistent connections: use HTTP/2 or keepalive HTTP/1.1 to avoid connection overhead at scale.
- Number of clients: ensure loadgen is not CPU-bound. Use multiple client hosts if needed.
- Request shapes: support variable input length distributions and KV-reuse scenarios.
- Deterministic inputs: store test prompts in versioned fixture files; every run consumes the same sequence in the same order unless testing randomness effects.

Example loadgen config (YAML-like):

---
model: llama-13b-qat
mode: open_loop
target_rps: 2000
clients: 8
keepalive: true
protocol: http2
seed: 20251110
input_pool: tests/fixtures/short-medium-long.json
prompt_distribution:
  short: 0.5
  medium: 0.3
  long: 0.2
max_tokens: 128
stop_on_error: false
warmup_seconds: 120
steady_state_seconds: 300
collect_traces: true
trace_sample_rate: 0.01
output: results/2025-11-10/llama-13b-qat-openloop.json
---

Warmup and steady-state guidance:
- Warmup purpose: allow the runtime to fill KV caches, trigger any lazy kernel compilation, and reach steady batching behavior.
- Minimum warmup: run at least 2x the observed JIT/compile time or a minimum of 60–120s (whichever is larger). For kernels that compile lazily, warmup until kernel compilation activity is negligible.
- Observe metrics during warmup: if GPU utilization or latency is still trending, extend warmup.
- Steady-state window: collect metrics over a window long enough to capture variability (recommended 300s).

Repeatability / reproducibility checklist:
- Source control: record runtime commit SHA, loadgen repo SHA, and model artifact checksum in results metadata.
- Environment: record AMI/container image ID, kernel version, CUDA/cudnn versions, NIC firmware, and host type (instance family).
- Isolation: run on isolated hosts (no other noisy tenants), or use cgroups to control background noise.
- Clock sync: ensure NTP/chrony running; timestamps matter for correlating traces.
- Fixed seeds: where randomness exists (temperature, sampling), use deterministic seeds for benchmarking.
- Multiple runs: perform >= 3 identical runs; report mean and standard deviation. Flag runs with >10% variance for investigation.

Data collection & instrumentation:
- Metrics exporters: Prometheus + node-exporter + DCGM exporter (for NVIDIA) to collect continuous telemetry.
- Tracing: sample full request traces (openTelemetry) at low rates to capture internal batching and scheduling delays.
- Profiling: when investigating bottlenecks, capture NVPROF/Nsight traces, and collect perf samples on CPU. Be aware of profiling overhead; profile separately from throughput runs where necessary.
- Logs: collect runtime logs at DEBUG level for selected runs (rotate after).
- Artifacts: save raw loadgen results (CSV/JSON), Prometheus scrape snapshots for the test period, and any trace/profiler outputs.

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them:
- Mistaking warmup for steady-state: verify plateau in GPU utilization and stable p99 before collecting.
- Client-side bottleneck: confirm load generators are not CPU or network-limited. Use multiple client machines and monitor client CPU/net.
- Connection churn: disabled keepalive will throttle RPS; ensure persistent connections for high RPS tests.
- Model cache effects: KV reuse or prefix caching can massively boost throughput for repeated prompts—document cache policy or use unique prompts when you want to measure worst-case.
- JIT/compile noise: first runs may include compilation; always warm up.
- Quantization variability: different quantization/pack formats can alter memory access patterns; measure separately and document quantization configs.
- Batch sizing artifacts: when saturation is reached, average batch size may jump; capture batch-size distribution.

Example commands (simplified):
- Run loadgen container:
  docker run --rm --net=host 
    -e LOADGEN_CONFIG=/cfg/llama-13b-openloop.yaml 
    -v $(pwd)/cfg:/cfg 
    ghcr.io/redwood-inference/rt-loadgen:sha-abcdef 
    /app/loadgen --config /cfg/llama-13b-openloop.yaml

- Snapshot Prometheus during run:
  curl -sS http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/export?start=<t0>&end=<t1> > run-2025-11-10-prom.json

- Collect NVML metrics:
  nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,power.draw,memory.used --format=csv -l 1 > nvml-llama13b.csv &

Analysis and reporting:
- Report must include: input distribution, model + runtime commit, hardware, warmup duration, steady-state window, per-run tokens/sec and latency percentiles, mean+stdev across runs, and artifact links (prometheus snapshot, traces, raw loadgen output).
- Plot time-series for tokens/sec and p99 during the entire run including warmup so reviewers can validate steady-state behavior.
- For regressions, compare kernel-level timelines and flamegraphs between baseline and regression.

When to run deeper profiling:
- If tokens/sec drops below expectation while GPU utilization is low -> suspect host-side scheduling, RPC overhead, or batching inefficiency.
- If p99 spikes despite high average throughput -> suspect queuing/backpressure or skewed batch formation.
- If GPU SM utilization is high but achieved tokens/sec is lower than baseline -> check memory bandwidth, kernel occupancy, and quantization code paths.

Acceptance for CI gating (proposal):
- Lightweight smoke: fast closed-loop test (30s) that validates basic correctness and a rough throughput sanity check on PRs touching batching or scheduler code.
- Nightly full harness: run longer open-loop scenarios against a staging cluster and record artifacts.
- Regression alerting: automatic comparison to baseline metrics; if tokens/sec regresses >5% and p99 regresses >10% raise an alert for eng-serving-runtime.

Quick checklist before publishing a benchmark run:
- [ ] Runtime, loadgen, model artifacts + checksums recorded
- [ ] Environment (image/driver/kernel/firmware) documented
- [ ] Warmup verified to reach plateau
- [ ] >=3 runs completed and variance computed
- [ ] Prometheus snapshot + trace samples archived
- [ ] Known cache/kv behaviors documented for the run

Next steps / TODOs:
- Add automated harness to Jenkins/GitHub Actions to run minimal smoke tests on PRs that touch scheduler or batching layers (JIRA-RT-1234).
- Flesh out regression dashboard with automated diff views (tokens/sec over time, p99) and links to artifacts.
- Build standardized fixtures for KV reuse patterns and prefix-heavy workloads.

Notes / context: this doc mixes best-practices we've used in-house with explicit warnings we learned from prior noisy benchmarks (client saturation, JIT noise, caching surprises). Keep this as the canonical internal reference for throughput benchmarking in serving runtime investigations.
